title: How to Choose Accounting Software
description: Choose accounting software by your transaction flow, reporting, tax jurisdiction, reconciliation, controls, migration and total cost. Includes a practical acceptance checklist for small businesses and finance teams.

sections.title: Introduction: Finding the Right Financial Foundation
sections.body: Accounting software is the system of record for financial transactions, so selection should start with how the business invoices, pays suppliers, reconciles accounts and closes each period. Define the reports the owner or accountant needs and identify jurisdiction-specific tax and filing requirements. The right product is the one that preserves accurate records and supports a repeatable close, not simply the one with the longest feature list.

sections.title: Assess Your Accounting Workflows
sections.body: Before evaluating any accounting software, document your complete financial workflow cycle. Start with how income enters your business ” do you send invoices and wait for payment, process payments at point of sale, bill on retainer or subscription basis, or a mix of methods? Each billing model requires different software capabilities. Invoice-based businesses need robust invoicing with customizable templates, recurring invoice automation, payment reminders, and online payment acceptance. Retail or point-of-sale businesses need real-time inventory tracking and payment terminal integration. Subscription businesses need recurring billing, dunning management, and revenue recognition support. Next, document your expense workflows ” how do employees submit expenses, how are bills from vendors processed and approved, and how are credit card transactions reconciled? Businesses with many employees submitting expenses need a platform with expense management features or integration with a dedicated expense tool like Expensify. Map your month-end close process: how are bank accounts reconciled, how are financial statements prepared, and who reviews them? The more manual steps in your current process, the more value you will get from automation features in new software. Finally, identify all integration requirements: payroll processing, payment processing (credit cards, ACH, wire transfers), CRM for invoicing from deals, project management for time-based billing, e-commerce platform for order-to-cash synchronization, and tax preparation software for seamless data export at filing time. Each integration reduces manual data entry and the risk of errors, but each also narrows the field of compatible platforms.

sections.title: Accounting Software Evaluation Scorecard
sections.body: Use this weighted scorecard to evaluate accounting platforms systematically. Adjust the weights based on your business type ” a service business that bills by the hour weights time tracking and invoicing higher, while a product business weights inventory and cost of goods sold tracking higher. Share this scorecard with your finance team and accountant before evaluating candidates.
rows: General ledger, accounts payable and receivable, bank reconciliation, financial statement generation (P&L, balance sheet, cash flow), chart of accounts customization, fiscal year management, multi-entity support

Customizable invoice templates, recurring invoice automation, online payment acceptance (credit card, ACH), payment reminders, client portal for invoice viewing and payment, batch invoicing, credit memos and refunds

Automatic bank feed connections for all business accounts, transaction categorization rules, real-time reconciliation suggestions, bank balance comparison, credit card import and categorization, receipt capture via mobile app

Custom report builder with date range and filter options, profit and loss by class or location, project profitability reporting, sales tax calculation and filing support, 1099 contractor management, tax preparation data export

Payroll system integration, payment processor integration, CRM sync for invoicing, project management time tracking import, e-commerce platform connection, expense management tool integration, API access for custom integrations
Learning curve for non-accountants, mobile app functionality, customer support quality during trial, user community size, documentation comprehensiveness, onboarding resources and guided setup

sections.title: Comparing Accounting Software Categories
sections.body: Accounting platforms fall into several categories based on their target market and feature depth. Understanding these categories helps you narrow your options before detailed evaluation. Entry-level platforms like Wave and ZipBooks offer free or very low-cost accounting for sole proprietors and freelancers with simple finances. Wave provides invoicing, receipt scanning, and basic accounting at no cost, with revenue from payment processing fees. These platforms work well for businesses with fewer than 10 transactions per month but lack inventory management, project profitability tracking, and robust reporting needed by growing businesses. Small business platforms like QuickBooks Online, Xero, and FreshBooks dominate the market for businesses with 1-50 employees. QuickBooks Online is the most widely adopted with the largest ecosystem of integrations, apps, and certified accountants. Xero offers a modern interface, unlimited users on most plans, and strong inventory management. FreshBooks excels at invoicing and time tracking for service-based businesses. All three connect to bank feeds, support online payments, and integrate with hundreds of third-party apps. Mid-market platforms like QuickBooks Enterprise and Sage Intacct add advanced capabilities like multi-entity consolidation, advanced inventory, project accounting, and role-based permissions for organizations with 50-500 employees. Enterprise ERP systems like NetSuite and Microsoft Dynamics 365 provide full accounting, supply chain management, CRM, and human resources in a unified platform for large organizations with complex financial operations. For most small to mid-sized businesses, the choice comes down to QuickBooks Online, Xero, or FreshBooks, with the deciding factors being ecosystem preference (QuickBooks has the largest network of accountants and apps), interface preference, and specific feature requirements like Xero's unlimited users or FreshBooks' superior invoicing experience.

sections.title: Total Cost of Ownership for Accounting Software
sections.body: Budget for subscription, transaction or payment fees, additional users, multi-currency or entity requirements, integrations, migration, training, support and internal administration. Include the cost of reconciling data between disconnected tools. Ask vendors to quote the same transaction volume, users, currencies, entities and reporting needs. Current prices are not independently verified in this guide; confirm current official terms before budgeting.

sections.title: Budget Recommendations by Business Type
sections.body: A freelancer with simple invoices may prioritize ease of use, bank reconciliation and accountant access. A service agency may need project profitability, retainers and reimbursable expenses. A retailer may need inventory and point-of-sale reconciliation. A multi-entity business may need consolidated reporting and stronger approval controls. These are workflow profiles, not price tiers; compare the exact plan against the requirements and get a written quote.

sections.title: Common Accounting Software Selection Mistakes
sections.body: Organizations frequently make these mistakes when choosing accounting software. Because financial data is sensitive and migration is complex, the cost of a wrong decision is higher than for most other software categories.
items: Choosing a platform without involving your accountant or bookkeeper ” your accountant likely has experience with multiple platforms and knows which ones generate the reports they need for tax preparation, financial analysis, and audit support

Underestimating the pain of data migration ” accounting data migration requires reconciling every account, ensuring all transactions are categorized correctly, and preserving audit trails. Expect migration to take 20-60 hours of your finance team's time plus potential professional fees

Focusing on monthly subscription price while ignoring payment processing fees ” a platform with a $10 lower monthly subscription may charge 1% higher payment processing, which costs more than the subscription savings if you process significant card payments

Overlooking bank feed reliability ” not all platforms connect reliably to all banks, and a platform that cannot maintain stable bank feeds creates manual reconciliation work that consumes hours each month. Check the platform's supported bank list and read recent reviews about feed reliability

Selecting a platform without mobile receipt capture ” if your team travels or makes purchases in the field, the ability to photograph receipts and have them automatically categorized and attached to expenses saves hours of data entry and prevents lost receipts at tax time

Choosing a platform that forces a specific chart of accounts structure ” your business has specific income and expense categories that match your industry and tax requirements, and a platform that limits account customization forces workarounds that complicate reporting

Ignoring user permission limitations ” if multiple team members need access to financial data, ensure the platform supports role-based permissions that control who can view, create, edit, approve, and export financial information at a granular level

sections.title: Accounting Software Decision Checklist
sections.body: Before migrating your financial data to a new accounting platform, verify each of these points with your finance team, accountant, and key stakeholders.
items: Have you tested the platform with your actual bank and credit card accounts to verify bank feed reliability and transaction categorization accuracy?
Does the platform support the invoicing format, payment terms, and online payment methods that your clients expect and your business requires?
Can the platform handle your chart of accounts structure including class tracking, location tracking, and custom income and expense categories?
Does the platform integrate with your payroll system or provide built-in payroll that meets your payroll tax filing and reporting needs?
Can the platform generate the financial reports your accountant needs for tax preparation, including profit and loss, balance sheet, and general ledger detail?
Does the platform support sales tax calculation and filing for all states where you have nexus, including automated rate updates and filing support?
Have you verified that the platform can import your historical transaction data including open invoices, unpaid bills, and year-to-date financials?
What is the total annual cost including subscription, payment processing fees, payroll add-on, and any connected app subscriptions you will need?
Does the platform provide a data export tool that can extract all transactions, attachments, and reports in standard formats for future migrations?
Have you checked platform reviews and talked to at least two businesses in your industry that have used the platform for over a year?

sections.title: Implementation and Data Migration Best Practices
sections.body: Accounting software implementation requires extra care because financial data must be accurate, complete, and auditable at all times. A single migration error can produce inaccurate financial statements, incorrect tax filings, or unreconciled bank accounts that take months to identify and correct. This is why thorough parallel testing is essential before cutting over from your old system. Follow a phased migration approach over 4-8 weeks, never rushing the go-live date. Phase 1 (Week 1): Set up the new platform's chart of accounts to match your current system. Configure tax rates, invoice templates, email settings, and user permissions. Connect bank feeds and verify transaction import accuracy. Phase 2 (Week 2): Import open accounts receivable (unpaid invoices) and open accounts payable (unpaid bills). Reconcile the totals against your current system to verify accuracy. Set up any recurring transactions like monthly subscriptions, rent, or loan payments. Phase 3 (Weeks 3-4): Run both systems in parallel for at least one full month-end close. Process all transactions in both platforms and compare the resulting financial statements. Every discrepancy must be investigated and resolved before cutting over. This parallel run is your insurance against migration errors that could affect tax filings or financial reporting. Phase 4 (Week 5): After the parallel run validates accuracy, migrate historical data for the current fiscal year. Year-to-date transactions, reconciled bank statements, and journal entries must be imported or recreated in the new system. Phase 5 (Week 6): Cut over to the new system and discontinue data entry in the old platform. Retain read-only access to the old system for reference. Notify clients of any changes to invoicing or payment portals. Schedule weekly check-ins with your finance team for the first month to address questions and refine workflows. The single most important rule: never delete or disable your old accounting system until you have completed at least one full month-end close in the new platform and reconciled all accounts.

sections.title: Frequently Asked Questions About Accounting Software
sections.body: Common questions: **Can I switch at year-end?** It may simplify opening balances, but timing depends on tax and reporting obligations; plan with the accountant. **What must be migrated?** Chart of accounts, contacts, opening balances, transactions and supporting records as required. **Is bank-feed support enough?** Test reconciliation exceptions and duplicate handling. **Can a payment platform replace accounting software?** Not necessarily; confirm which system is the general ledger. **How do I compare costs?** Include implementation, integrations, fees and administration.
items: **What is the difference between accounting software and bookkeeping software?** Accounting software handles the full financial cycle including general ledger, accounts payable and receivable, financial statements, and tax reporting. Bookkeeping software focuses on transaction recording, categorization, and reconciliation. Most modern accounting platforms like QuickBooks and Xero include both accounting and bookkeeping functionality. Dedicated bookkeeping tools like Bench offer human-assisted categorization and reporting.

**Can I use accounting software without accounting knowledge?** Yes, but with limitations. Platforms like FreshBooks and Wave are designed for non-accountants with intuitive interfaces for invoicing, expense tracking, and basic reporting. However, you will need an accountant or bookkeeper for tasks like chart of accounts setup, month-end close, financial statement review, and tax preparation. Most platforms offer accountant access levels so your professional can review and adjust entries.

**How often should I reconcile my accounts?** Ideally weekly, but at minimum monthly before closing the period. Frequent reconciliation catches errors early, prevents bank feed disconnections from creating backlogs, and ensures your financial statements are accurate for decision-making. Most accounting platforms make reconciliation straightforward by matching imported bank transactions to entered records.

**What is the best accounting software for a small business with inventory?** QuickBooks Online Plus and Xero Established both offer robust inventory tracking including purchase orders, stock level management, cost of goods sold calculation, and inventory valuation reports. QuickBooks has a larger ecosystem of inventory apps for barcode scanning and low-stock alerts. For businesses with complex inventory needs, dedicated inventory management software integrated with accounting is recommended.

**How do I handle sales tax in accounting software?** Most platforms support sales tax tracking by setting up tax rates per product or service and per jurisdiction. They calculate tax on invoices and generate sales tax liability reports. Some platforms like QuickBooks Online offer automated sales tax calculation and filing through a paid add-on service. For businesses selling in multiple states, automated sales tax software like Avalara or TaxJar integrates with most major accounting platforms.

**Can I switch accounting software mid-year?** Yes, but it is more complex than switching at year-end because you need to migrate year-to-date transactions and ensure the new platform's beginning balances match your current system's ending balances. Plan a parallel run for at least one month to validate accuracy. Many businesses choose to switch at the start of a new fiscal year to simplify the transition, but mid-year migration is feasible with careful planning.

**What integrations are essential for accounting software?** The most important integrations are your bank accounts (for automatic transaction import), payment processor (for automatic reconciliation of settled transactions), payroll system (for payroll journal entries), and e-commerce platform if applicable (for order-to-cash synchronization). CRM integration for invoicing from deals and expense management integration for employee expense reports are valuable but secondary.

**How do I ensure my accounting data is secure?** Verify that your platform uses bank-level encryption (AES-256), supports multi-factor authentication, provides role-based user permissions, and maintains a complete audit log of all changes. Most major platforms also offer read-only access for accountants and view-only access for stakeholders. Request the vendor's SOC 2 Type II report and review their data backup and disaster recovery practices.

**What is the typical ROI of accounting software?** Businesses typically save 5-15 hours per month on bookkeeping tasks by switching from manual processes to accounting software. For a business paying a bookkeeper $30-50 per hour, this represents $150-$750 in monthly savings from reduced bookkeeping hours alone. Additional savings come from faster invoicing (reducing days sales outstanding by 5-15 days), better expense tracking (capturing previously missed deductions), and reduced tax preparation fees.

**Should I choose cloud or on-premise accounting software?** Cloud accounting software dominates for businesses of all sizes due to lower upfront costs, automatic updates, anywhere access, bank feed connectivity, and integration with other cloud tools. On-premise software like QuickBooks Desktop is only recommended for businesses with unreliable internet access, strict data residency requirements, or legacy workflows that depend on specific desktop features that cloud versions lack. For 95% of businesses, cloud accounting is the right choice.

sections.title: Pilot worksheet and acceptance criteria
sections.body: Run one representative workflow from beginning to end and record the exact input, expected result, observed result, manual work, failure cases, permissions, export and owner. Agree on acceptance criteria before vendor demonstrations. Use pass, partial pass, fail or unknown rather than a numeric score without evidence. Check current product documentation and a dated quote for any feature, price or limit that materially affects the decision. Assign a person to maintain the configuration, review access and revisit the decision after the rollout.

author: Emily Nakamura
